name: Wealth Strategy Playbook
tag: Helps veterans plan the buy, borrow, die strategy with holding-company structures.

scenarios.title: Fund living costs without selling
scenarios.ask: Show how a ${value} rental portfolio with {owed} owed could fund living costs without selling, using a {ltv} credit line.
steps: A line of credit at {ltv} could release about ${=max(0, round(value * (ltv - owed) / 100))}, drawn over 5 years.
Checked a {drop} price drop with the line fully drawn: loan-to-value becomes {=round(max(owed, ltv) / max(1, 100 - drop) * 100)}%.
Showed how a holding company can separate the properties from personal assets.

result.title: Illustration only
rows: Review with your CPA and attorney

followups: What if I already owe more than the line allows?
Then the line releases nothing until the portfolio grows or the debt is paid down. The playbook shows how many years that might take at sample growth rates.

It depends on the lender's limits. If {=round(max(owed, ltv) / max(1, 100 - drop) * 100)}% is above what your lender allows, you could be asked to pay down the line. The playbook flags this before you draw.

scenarios.title: Design a holding-company structure
scenarios.ask: I own {props} properties and run {biz} businesses. Show a holding structure that keeps them separate.
steps: Drew a sample chart: trust at the top, a holding company, then property and business LLCs.
Placed {props} properties into {=ceil(props / per_llc)} property LLCs with up to {per_llc} each.
Kept {biz} operating businesses in their own LLCs, apart from the real estate.
Listed bank accounts, insurance and agreements each entity needs.

result.title: Sample structure
rows: {=ceil(props / per_llc) + biz + 2} including trust and holding company
Educational model; have an attorney set up your structure

followups: Why not one LLC for everything?
If one property has a claim, assets in the same LLC can be exposed. Splitting them limits how far one problem can reach, at the cost of more paperwork.
Yes. Most states charge formation and annual fees, and each entity needs its own books. The playbook adds those costs to the plan.

scenarios.title: Plan for veteran household goals
scenarios.ask: Our household needs ${need} a year from the portfolio for {years} years. What would that draw look like?
steps: Estimated interest if the balance builds and interest is paid each year.
Compared draws with sample rental income, so you see how much the rents cover.
Listed questions for your CPA, attorney and VA-accredited advisor if benefits are involved.

result.title: Illustration only
rows: Not financial advice; numbers are illustrative

followups: Why does interest grow every year?
Each year adds a new draw to the balance, so interest is charged on more money. By year {years}, interest is about ${=round(need * years * rate / 100)} a year.
The playbook does not determine benefits. If you receive needs-based benefits, ask a VA-accredited representative how borrowing or assets are treated.
